{{Commonscat|Rhaphiolepis umbellata}} 

'''''Rhaphiolepis umbellata''''' or '''Sexton's bride'''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sexton's Bride (Rhaphiolepis umbellata) |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/367951-Rhaphiolepis-umbellata |access-date=2024-11-19 |website=iNaturalist |language=en}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Rosaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to Korea, Japan and Taiwan. Growing to {{convert|1.5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall and wide, it is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] with glossy oval leaves, and scented white flowers, sometimes tinged with pink, in early summer.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Rhaphiolepis umbellata''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1598|accessdate=30 May 2013}}</ref> It is used in Japan as an astringent and a dyeing agent. The bark contains [[(−)-catechin 7-O-β-d-glucopyranoside]] and [[(+)-catechin 5-0-β-d-glucopyranoside]].<ref name=Nonaka>{{cite journal |title=Flavanol glucosides from rhubarb and ''Rhaphiolepis umbellata'' |author=Gen-Ichiro Nonaka |author2=Emiko Ezakia |author3=Katsuya Hayashia |author4=Itsuo Nishioka |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=22 |issue=7 |year=1983 |pages=1659–61 |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(83)80105-8|bibcode=1983PChem..22.1659N }}</ref>

==Uses==
Known as Sharinbai (車輪梅) in Japan and as Techigi in [[Amami Oshima]], this plant is used to create a dye to create the highly valued [[Ōshima-tsumugi]] kimono.
The bark of the tree is chopped into chips and boiled for over 10 hours. This tannin rich decoction serves as a dye for the silk threads. After dyeing, the threads are then dyed in mud from paddy fields rich in iron content for post-mordanting until they turn black. <ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.tumugi.co.jp/english/index.html | title=About Ooshima Tsumugimura｜Ooshima Tsumugi Mura }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Oshima Tsumugi and Mud Dyeing|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/common/001564412.pdf}}</ref>

Additionally, due to its resilience to drying and air pollution, Sharinbai trees are planted along roadsides. Their glossy evergreen leaves make them suitable for garden planting, enduring well against frequent pruning.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.919g.co.jp/blog/?p=4915 | title=花咲く生垣におすすめ「シャリンバイ（車輪梅）」 – お庭から始まる豊かなグリーンライフ「庭サポ」 }}</ref>

Unlike most of ''Rhaphiolepis'' species, its fruits are inedible.
